closure_audit.original_abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and their meta-analyses remain the foundation of evidence-based psychotherapy, yet many of them are currently limited by methodological weaknesses, conceptual confusion, and interpretive challenges. This review first clarifies key distinctions-between response and effect, between minimal important change (MIC) and smallest worthwhile difference (SWD), and between absolute versus relative effect measures-showing how these distinctions contribute to valid interpretation of treatment outcomes. We argue for odds ratios (ORs) and standardized mean differences (SMDs) as the most generalizable summary indices, to be supplemented with control and experimental event rates (CER&EER) by MIC-based thresholds for clinical interpretability. Advances in evidence synthesis, particularly individual participant data (IPD) and component network meta-analyses (NMA), enable the identification of effect modifiers and the isolation of efficacious therapeutic components, although they face challenges of data availability, harmonization, and reporting standards. To strengthen the evidence base further, larger and more efficient trials are needed. Platform trials and master protocols, drawing on shared controls and adaptive features, promise greater efficiency and comparability, as exemplified by the RESiLIENT digitally centralized trial of smartphone-based CBT. Such designs, combined with adaptive interventions and AI-driven personalization, illustrate how psychotherapy research can move beyond small, fragmented RCTs towards scalable precision medicine.

Highlights

Abstract
Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and their meta-analyses remain the foundation of evidence-based psychotherapy, yet many of them are currently limited by methodological weaknesses, conceptual confusion, and interpretive challenges. This review first clarifies key distinctions—between response and effect, between minimal important change (MIC) and smallest worthwhile difference (SWD), and between absolute versus relative effect measures—showing how these distinctions contribute to valid interpretation of treatment outcomes. We argue for odds ratios (ORs) and standardized mean differences (SMDs) as the most generalizable summary indices, to be supplemented with control and experimental event rates (CER&EER) by MIC-based thresholds for clinical interpretability. Advances in evidence synthesis, particularly individual participant data (IPD) and component network meta-analyses (NMA), enable the identification of effect modifiers and the isolation of efficacious therapeutic components, although they face challenges of data availability, harmonization, and reporting standards. To strengthen the evidence base further, larger and more efficient trials are needed. Platform trials and master protocols, drawing on shared controls and adaptive features, promise greater efficiency and comparability, as exemplified by the RESiLIENT digitally centralized trial of smartphone-based CBT. Such designs, combined with adaptive interventions and AI-driven personalization, illustrate how psychotherapy research can move beyond small, fragmented RCTs towards scalable precision medicine.

Introduction
It is widely accepted that randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and their meta-analyses (MAs) constitute the cornerstone of evidence-based practices.
The number of publications in psychotherapy has been rising exponentially when queried with keywords “Psychotherapy[Mesh]” in PubMed (Fig. 1). Against this background, the number and proportion of RCTs have increased since 1960s, from 1% in 1960s to 23% in 2025. However, the total number as well as the proportion appear to have plateaued since 2010 at around 20%. By contrast, since its first appearance in 1990, the number and proportion of MAs are constantly growing, reaching 8% in 2025.
Unfortunately there are many problems with psychotherapy trials and, consequently, with their meta-analyses, starting from infrequent preregistration (Shinohara et al., 2015), small sample sizes (Cuijpers et al., 2024), variations in control conditions (Michopoulos et al., 2021; Watts et al., 2015), performance bias due to the open nature of psychotherapy, assessment bias (Miguel et al., 2025), and limited reproducibility (Furukawa, 2014; Open Science Collaboration, 2015).
We need to address these and other issues so that we can estimate the effects of the psychotherapies properly through RCTs and MAs. The purpose of this paper however is not to make a comprehensive list of these problems or adequately discuss them. Instead, this article addresses more fundamental conceptual and terminological confusion in the current literature concerning treatment effects, and uses this unified approach to advance precision medicine and personalized psychotherapy. We start with the key distinction between response (within-group change) and effect (between-group difference) and the corresponding concepts of the minimal important change (MID) and the smallest worthwhile difference (SWD). We then move on to the various indexes of treatment effect, including relative and absolute indexes, and examine which indexes are more generalizable and interpretable and which should therefore be used in expressing treatment effects. By understanding this framework we can correctly distinguish between prognostic factors and effect modifiers in the construction of precision medicine models. New advances in meta-analyses can contribute to personalized psychotherapies using this framework but also have their difficulties. Better and larger trials are needed. We finally argue that new trial designs such as the platform trial, decentralized trial and adaptive trial, with their large sample sizes, harmonized outcomes and shared control(s), can boost trial efficacy and scale, thus ultimately contributing to the evidence base necessary for personalized psychotherapies.

How can we improve psychotherapies through evidence synthesis?
I hope it is now clear to the readers that the ultimate outputs of evidence synthesis must include OR or SMD, and corresponding CER/EER using MIC (or similar constructs) and, where possible, the same indices for meaningful subgroups of individuals (precision medicine).
After all, we need better and larger RCTs but how can we do more of them?
Learning that there are so many problems with currently available trials of psychotherapy and that combining them can only solve a few of them (while exposing new difficulties), it seems that we need better and larger RCTs to obtain meaningful ORs/SMDs and corresponding CER/EER for important subgroups.
Concluding remarks
Psychotherapies need stronger evidence base to improve their effectiveness. First, we have to know how effectiveness is to be expressed to avoid confusion, enhance generalizability and help interpretability. Several evidence synthetic approaches can distill useful knowledge from the available database of randomized trials.
